title: AI Can Cut Film Budgets by Up to 40%, Says ‘The Outlaws’ Director Kang Yoon-sung, as Netflix Reveals Use on 300 Titles: ‘A Human Touch Is Absolutely Essential’
description: Netflix has used AI in one form or another on some 300 of its titles, Lee Sung-gyun, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, told an audi
body:
Netflix has used AI in one form or another on some 300 of its titles, Lee Sung-gyun, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, told an audience at the Busan International Film Festival. 

	On the same panel, “The Outlaws” director Kang Yoon-sung said AI workflows could take 30% to 40% off a feature film’s production budget.

	Lee shared the stage with Kang and Kimball Thurston, chief technology officer at Wētā FX, for “Film Production and AI: New Tools, New Possibilities.” Netflix and the MPA co-hosted the session. It was part of Creative Asia, the Netflix and BIFF program for emerging Asian talent. Film critic Yun Sung-eun moderated.
	

	“Across around 300 Netflix titles, AI has actually been put to use in various ways,” Lee said. “It’s being used in previs, in production design, in working out set-dressing concepts ahead of time, in editorial, and of course in VFX.”


	Lee said new technology has always startled people when it arrives. “All these technological changes and new tools have helped a great deal with the ‘how,’ how we make what we make better, but they never decided the ‘why,’ why we have to tell this story,” he said. “AI is the same.”

	He also screened a reel from Eyeline, Netflix’s VFX studio, about what the company calls hybrid production, which mixes live-action photography, VFX and generative tools. A second clip showed AI and VFX together producing large crowd scenes for the Netflix India title “Glory.” Lee said that under tight budgets and schedules, those scenes would normally have had to be dropped.
	

	Kang co-directed “Run to the West” with AI filmmaker Kwon Han-seul. The film opened in Korean cinemas last October and was billed as Korea’s first feature to use AI across its entire production. Kang turned to AI there as a substitute for CG. “At the time, AI technology was at a really rudimentary, low level, so we mainly used it for compositing and making creatures,” he said. “And back then, even the creatures didn’t blend well with the footage we’d shot.” In just a year, he said, AI’s quality has reached the point where using it commercially is no problem at all.

	His test clip for “The Gulf of Aden,” a film built around military operations at sea, was made entirely with AI earlier this year using Kling, the Chinese software. Kang said the test was rendered at reduced quality. Current tools, he said, can output 4K at 10-bit color or higher, which is enough for cinemas.

	An audience member asked about cost. “When we calculated how much we’d save on ‘The Gulf of Aden’ for fundraising, it came to an actual reduction of around 40%,” Kang said. “That’s not just from replacing CG and VFX. The shoot itself got simpler, and it cut the overall production period to some extent.”

	Kang said AI has put projects that collapsed at the budget stage back on the table. That opens the door to genre and sci-fi films at a time when the Korean industry is struggling to grow. But he also said that because AI handles so much of the creative work, it often cuts out the discussion, effort and experience of many people that filmmaking has always relied on, leaving images made from one person’s ideas alone. “So the quality of the footage AI makes is very high, but when it comes to delivering emotion and moving audiences, I think we’re in a period where it has actually gotten worse,” he said.

	Lee said he related strongly to Kang’s point. Some things now come out with a single click, he said, “but when it comes to conveying emotion, ultimately a human has to touch it once more. I strongly agree that a human touch is absolutely essential.”

	Thurston described the deep learning denoiser behind his second Academy Scientific and Technical Award as “assistive AI.” “It is basically not allowed to change the creative intent in any way,” he said. “It touches pixels, but it only fixes them.”
	

	He said Wētā has used machine learning for at least a decade, or 20 to 25 years if you count early forms of Massive, the system it built for “The Lord of the Rings.” He also flagged gaps in color accuracy. “If all your AI models have been trained on video images, you’re not getting the right red for a Coca-Cola can,” Thurston said. “You get Netflix red, but not Coca-Cola.”

	Asked how the companies keep pace with new models, Lee said Netflix works under strict internal guidelines and tests new tools before adopting them. “If you’re asking about speed, I’d like to say that we’re not wildly obsessed with it,” he said. Thurston said Wētā is building an open-source tool through the Academy Software Foundation to track AI use and provenance, designed to link with initiatives such as C2PA.

	On sustainability, Thurston said Wētā’s data center in Wellington, New Zealand, which uses closed-loop cooling, now draws “zero liters of water per year.” Lee said Netflix looks at sustainability company-wide, including its 2030 goal to cut carbon emissions, and doesn’t study AI’s impact separately.

	Kang expects AI use to split in two directions. Short-form content will focus on productivity, and he pointed to China, where some short-form projects are made entirely with AI from planning to distribution. Film and drama will focus instead on credibility. He also showed footage from a feature animation he is developing, with photoreal backgrounds and animated characters he wants to move like live-action actors.

	On replacing actors, Kang said it would be difficult. “No matter how much AI technology advances, actors are creators who deliver emotion and move the audience,” he said. “Even if AI acting becomes very sophisticated and imitates very precisely, emotion doesn’t come through because of its mechanical coldness.” He sees AI’s role in stunt and stand-in work instead.

	Thurston agreed. “The point is not to replace actors, right? No way,” he said. “We are audiovisual storytellers, and storytelling is studying the human condition.”

	Lee closed the session by saying technology will keep changing, and surprising, even shocking, videos will keep coming out. “But in the end, it’s humans who will write, and what we want more of is stories told by humans,” he said.

schema.headline: AI Can Cut Film Budgets by Up to 40%, Says ‘The Outlaws’ Director Kang Yoon-sung, as Netflix Reveals Use on 300 Titles: ‘A Human Touch Is Absolutely Essential’

title: Busan Market Chief Ellen Y.D. Kim Plots Year-Round ACFM 365 Platform, Warns Public Funding Has Stalled
description: The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) should grow beyond its four days in Busan into a platform that runs all year, director Ellen Y.D. Kim tells
body:
The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) should grow beyond its four days in Busan into a platform that runs all year, director Ellen Y.D. Kim tells Variety. She adds that public money for the market has not grown alongside it.

	Kim calls the idea ACFM 365. It would be a permanent database and matchmaking service that joins the market data in The A Report with the matching work now done by the Asian Project Market (APM) and the Busan Story Market.
	

	Her five-year targets include regular publication of The A Report and a standing leaders’ forum built on The A Summit. She also wants Cinema by Brand to become a financing model of its own and the Asian Cinema Fund to partner with international funds. More delegates from Latin America, the Arab world and Africa could lift the number of countries represented past 60, and possibly above 70.


	“The biggest obstacle is funding,” Kim says. “The scale and the role of the market have grown quickly, but public support has not kept pace. National funding for ACFM has stayed at the same level for two years running. The film industry is small in scale, but it is the front-runner that opens the way for other industries. Supporting film is an investment, not a subsidy, and a market needs to be understood as industry infrastructure, not as an event.”

	ACFM is in its 21st edition this year. Last year, industry registration rose 14.4% and overall attendance rose 13.5%. This year there are 339 exhibiting companies and institutions from 32 countries and territories, 17% more than last year. Tech exhibitors went from seven to 18, and national agencies and film commissions from 62 to 79. Thailand, the market’s first Country of Honor, has 28 exhibitors. Japan, the ProducerHub Focus Country, has 46.
	

	Kim credits curation for the growth. The market kept its core strands and added ProducerHub, InnoAsia, Doc Square and The A, and these drew people who had never attended a market before. This year’s additions include an Investor Summit, microdrama sessions and Cinema by Brand, which pairs film productions with brand partners.

	“The core is cinema,” Kim says. “The Sales Market, APM and the Asian Cinema Fund are the backbone of ACFM, and that structure will not change.” She applies one test to any new program: whether it widens the opportunities for cinema.

	“Visibility and revenue are different things,” Kim says. “For much of the Asian content that has succeeded globally, most of the IP and the revenue belong to global platforms or studios.”

	In her view, producers need to keep their IP and trade it directly. The Busan Story Market is built for that, and ProducerHub has become a place where producers from across the region discuss creators’ rights and recoupment.

	Korea’s numbers look healthy at first glance. First-half box office rose 42% on last year, admissions rose 34%, and Korean films took 64% of revenue. But there were 22 fewer Korean releases, and Korean commercial films averaged a return of minus 33% in 2025.

	“Producers say they cannot find money; investors say there are no projects to invest in,” Kim says. “I see this as a rebound, not yet a structural recovery.”

	As a result, Korean producers now plan international pre-sales and co-productions from the development stage. The Asian Producers Alliance, led by the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and the Association of Indonesian Film Producers (APROFI), will announce its launch at ProducerHub.

	New money is also arriving from outside film. Kim points to a conglomerate in India, broadcaster joint ventures in Thailand, mining companies in Mongolia and a beverage brand in China, all of which are backing films. In Taiwan, telecom and media companies have formed joint funds with a public agency. Public money remains the base, through Korea’s Fund of Funds film account, Malaysia’s production rebate and funds in Singapore and Taiwan. But Kim notes that it shifts when policy does.

	Streamers are moving from licensing rights to co-financing production, according to country reports in The A Report. In the Philippines, only 32 of 88 first-half releases played in cinemas. In Korea, an industry agreement on holdback windows that was targeted for August did not happen.
	

	One year after InnoAsia’s launch, Mateo AI Studio has raised KRW2 billion ($1.5 million) in pre-Series A funding. The AI feature “Steelay” will be previewed at this year’s Work-in-Progress Showcase and opens in Korean cinemas on Oct. 20. This year’s theme is “Cinema Coevolves with Tech.”

	“What concerns me is that institutions and people are not keeping up with the speed of the technology,” Kim says. She also worries that junior crew could lose their training ground if their jobs are automated first. “And if Asia does not own the models trained on Asian languages and images, the IP problem we lived through in the platform era will repeat itself.”

	Kim produced “Cry Woman” and “Hanaan.” She tried to co-produce “Hanaan” internationally, but it ended up a solely Korean production shot in Uzbekistan. Today she sees co-productions forming between Asian countries, including a three-way project from Thailand’s M Studio, Japan’s Toei and Korea’s Showbox, and the first financial co-production between Korea and Mongolia. Treaties between Asian countries are still rare.

	“Co-production used to be an option; now it is an essential strategy for sharing risk,” Kim says.

	The Asian Cinema Fund’s Co-Production Support Fund chose three projects this year, including the new film from Fukada Koji. This year 10 Japanese producers will also pitch projects, including co-productions with Korea, Canada, Indonesia and France.

	Asked why companies should come to Busan rather than Cannes, Berlin, Hong Kong or Tokyo, Kim points to the festival and the city. “Busan has the Busan International Film Festival, where the sea, cinema and stars come together, and ACFM is held alongside it. For people who have been coming to the festival for many years, Busan has become something like a hometown: a place with flavors they miss, films they miss and people they miss,” she says. 

	 She also notes that international participants outnumber Korean ones. “For anyone who wants to work with Asia, there is no place as efficient over four days,” she says. “Projects that pass through APM and the Asian Cinema Fund turn up at major festivals a few years later. Busan is where you can meet those films first, at the development stage. Companies from Europe and the Americas know this too, and for them Busan is the gateway to Asia.”

schema.headline: Busan Market Chief Ellen Y.D. Kim Plots Year-Round ACFM 365 Platform, Warns Public Funding Has Stalled

title: Vietnamese Supernatural Horror ‘Bloodline: The Curse Within’ Heads to Busan Market With Mockingbird Pictures (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Vietnamese supernatural horror film “Bloodline: The Curse Within” will be introduced to international buyers by Mockingbird Pictures at the Asian Co
body:
Vietnamese supernatural horror film “Bloodline: The Curse Within” will be introduced to international buyers by Mockingbird Pictures at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the market of the Busan International Film Festival.

	The company holds worldwide distribution rights to the film, which will open in theaters across Vietnam on Dec. 25. Directed by Đinh Đức Thiện and produced by K8 Studio and Hoàng Gia, the picture is known locally as “Huyết Thống.”
	

	The story follows a celebrated pediatric heart surgeon whose daughter falls prey to a vengeful ghost. When medicine can do nothing against an age-old curse, he must turn the scalpel he has used to save lives on his own buried sins. The ghost itself has its roots in that long-hidden past.


	Award-winning actor Quách Ngọc Ngoan leads the cast. He drew acclaim for his lead turn in Victor Vu’s “The Immortal” (“Người Bất Tử”) and was most recently seen in the hit “The Journey of Heroes” (“Trại Buôn Người”). He is joined by Quang Tuấn, a familiar face in Vietnamese horror who fronts “The Corpse” franchise, and Lan Phương, who appeared in “Phi Phong: The Blood Demon,” the biggest-grossing Vietnamese horror title to date.

	“The supernatural is only one half of ‘Bloodline,’” said director Đinh Đức Thiện. “What interested me was placing medicine and spirituality side by side, while exploring what people are willing to sacrifice when someone they love is threatened.”

	Hoàng Gia previously led development on “The Corpse 2” (“Quỷ Nhập Tràng 2”). He said the team wanted the film to be genuinely frightening, “while grounding the horror in something deeply human – family, blood ties and the consequences passed from one generation to the next.”
	

	Mockingbird will present the title to buyers and distributors in Busan as part of its newest lineup of Vietnamese films. Phong Duong, the company’s business director, also serves as a co-executive producer on the project.

	“Audiences today expect more from horror than a strong concept – they expect quality in every aspect of the filmmaking,” Duong said. “With ‘Bloodline: The Curse Within,’ we see that ambition in the storytelling, performances and overall cinematic experience, and that is the kind of Vietnamese cinema we want to bring to the world.”

	Mockingbird works to push Vietnamese and Southeast Asian films into markets outside their home territories. Each year it handles upwards of 60 theatrical releases and more than 100 titles for post-theatrical windows, covering horror, comedy, romance and action. A growing share of its lineup is made up of standout hits and record-setters with appeal beyond their home market.

schema.headline: Vietnamese Supernatural Horror ‘Bloodline: The Curse Within’ Heads to Busan Market With Mockingbird Pictures (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus
description: Netflix research found that 67% of surveyed members internationally expressed interest in visiting South Korea. For the streamer’s Sung Q Lee, the p
body:
Netflix research found that 67% of surveyed members internationally expressed interest in visiting South Korea. For the streamer’s Sung Q Lee, the pull lies in the stories set there, rather than the scenery alone.

	Lee, Netflix’s senior director of APAC production, made the case at the opening masterclass of Creative Asia, which Netflix and the 31st Busan International Film Festival brought back for a third consecutive year on Oct. 10.
	

	Held at Dongseo University’s Centum Campus, the program was developed with the Asian Film Commissions Network and the Motion Picture Association. This year’s edition added workshops led by Netflix executives alongside masterclasses and industry panels.


	Moderated by Busan Asian Film School professor James Bang, the opening session, on how locations shape storytelling, also featured location manager Lauren Cooper and “Perfect Days” co-producer Kunieda Reiko.

	Cooper said she first reads a script as an audience member before considering its demands as a location manager, and works closely with the production designer. “Filmmaking is like a team sport,” she said. “You need great flexibility to work with the crew and the story.”

	Kunieda quoted Wim Wenders: “The artifice of a story can ruin a film.” The director resists imposing predetermined themes or concepts, she said. On “Perfect Days,” which was shot in 16 days, the story was allowed to develop organically from its locations.

	“Location and storytelling are not separable,” Kunieda said, describing production’s role in translating creative ambitions into filmmaking.
	

	Citing the Jeju-set “When Life Gives You Tangerines,” he said universal emotions connect audiences to unfamiliar places.

schema.headline: Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus

title: Vietnamese Horror ‘Arithmadtic’ Leads Bee Entertainment’s Busan Market Slate, With New Film From ‘The Corpse’ Director
description: Psychological horror “Arithmadtic,” set in an elite international school, leads a genre-heavy slate that Vietnam’s Bee Entertainment is presenting t
body:
Psychological horror “Arithmadtic,” set in an elite international school, leads a genre-heavy slate that Vietnam’s Bee Entertainment is presenting to buyers at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

	Vietnamese films grossed more than VND3 trillion ($114 million) at home in 2025, outperforming international titles in the local market for the first time. Bee is aiming to take that momentum abroad.


	Its slate pairs four features, all set for release in 2027, with three long-form TV dramas at various stages of production. The company is using the market to find partners for investment, co-development and distribution, as well as rights licensing deals.
	

	Anh Thu, known for the 2007 Vietnam-South Korea co-production “Muoi: The Legend of a Portrait,” and Lam Thanh My (“Yellow Flowers on the Green Grass”) star in “Arithmadtic,” or “Cong Tru Nhan Chia” in Vietnamese. The film’s campus is styled after the Dark Academia aesthetic. The story centers on a transfer student’s enigmatic bond with a teacher, as a string of unexplained, supernatural incidents cracks the school’s polished facade.

	Phuong Tra My, who played the lead in “The Third Wife,” which premiered at Toronto and won the NETPAC Award, joins the cast alongside Chu Anh Tuan, Cong Ninh, Hoang Minh Hung and Dac Thang. The film is directed by Irving Ly, whose short “Close the Eye to See” played BFI Flare and the Korea Queer Film Festival and won a Silver Kite at Vietnam’s 2025 Golden Kite Awards. It opens in January 2027.

	Three more features are set for release across 2027. Tran Nhan Kien, who trained at the Asian Film School and took part in the Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival’s B.I.G NAFF Fantastic Film School, directs “The Step-Mother.” It follows a boy who has lost his father, as his relationship with his stepmother moves from conflict and misunderstanding to the blurry line between strictness and care. It is dated for the second quarter.
	

	Pom Nguyen directed “The Corpse” franchise, whose first two installments grossed more than VND280 billion ($10.7 million) combined. Next up from Pom Nguyen is “How to Find a Fortune in 60 Days,” which combines action, comedy and family drama, due in the third quarter. Le Ha Nguyen’s “Dealing With a Ghost,” a horror romantic comedy, closes the film slate with a fourth-quarter release.

	On the series side, “The Unrecognized Heir,” an 80-episode family drama directed by Trac Huynh Nhat Tan, began airing on VTV9 in December 2025 and has already drawn 1 billion views across social media platforms, according to the company. “A Deal With God,” a 65-episode series directed by Dang Minh Quoc, mixes family drama with comedy and fantasy. Trac also directs “Destined to Find You,” an 80-episode romance now in post-production.

	A subsidiary of Bee Comm, Bee Entertainment invests in, produces, releases and sells both Vietnamese and foreign films. Founded in 2009, Bee Comm produces the Vietnamese edition of “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” and the social-impact program “Mai Am Gia Dinh Viet” (“The Vietnamese Family Shelter”).

	The ACFM runs through Oct. The 31st Busan International Film Festival closes Oct. 15.

schema.headline: Vietnamese Horror ‘Arithmadtic’ Leads Bee Entertainment’s Busan Market Slate, With New Film From ‘The Corpse’ Director

title: Movistar Plus Drives Into YA Comedy, Smart Social Issue Genre
description: Over the last two years, no Spanish company has helped drive Spanish content onto the world stage more than Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish pay T
body:
Over the last two years, no Spanish company has helped drive Spanish content onto the world stage more than Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish pay TV/SVOD operator.

	Since 2025 alone, Movistar Plus Originals have scored the two top prizes at Series Mania with “Querer” and “Celeste,” has earned two Oscar nominations with “Sirāt,” while “La Bola Negra,” another Original, has emerged as the Cannes Festival’s biggest Oscar contender.
	

	Last week, Movistar Plus garnered International Emmy nominations for Alberto Rodríguez’s “The Anatomy of a Moment” and best actor for Javier Cámara in “Jakarta.”


	Such plaudits raise the question of how Movistar Plus moves forward from here. Its key Mipcom titles supply some answers.

	Under a new management team — CEO Alfonso Gómez Palacio and contents director Juan Andrés García Romero — Movistar Plus is attempting to reach out to younger audiences. It’s scored one home run, Mipcom title “Many People Need to Die,” the series debut from YouTube-podcast comedian Victoria Martín. A withering take on Millennial angst, it has been an audience and new subscriber driver, says García Romero, noting that Movistar Plus has already ordered a Season 2.

	Shot in Catalonia’s heavenly Aran Valley, “Killing a Bear,” another top Mipcom title, underscores another strategic drive: co-production.

	Created by Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“Crematorium,” “The Zone”), the fact-based wild bear murder mystery that exposes the deep social conflict in the high Pyrenees marks the fourth co-production between Movistar Plus and broadcast network Arte France. Season 2 of “Celeste,” also a Movistar Plus original and another Spanish Mipcom buzz pick, is co-produced with the Mediapro Studio, with the Mediapro Studio Distribution handling international sales.
	

	Movistar Plus‘’’ overseas breakout has rolled off its close relationships with many of Spain’s greatest younger auteurs, giving them the resources to make the films and TV series they envision at a competitive level of across-the-board production values comparable to, for example, France.

	On “Celeste” Season 1, ”we were given a marvellous degrees of creative freedom. It could have become a madcap comedy full of gags and jokes made for the broadest of audiences. Instead, we were even encouraged to make a series with light and shade,” says “Celeste” creator Diego San Jose.

	That strategy has proved highly successful. In early July, Movistar Plus created waves when it announced that it will double its original Spanish series annual output from eight to 16 titles. “Originals attract more client and generate more engagement,” Movistar Plus noted.

	In order to make such series, the pay TV operator has to bring on emerging talent alongside the creatives it already engages. “The Castle,” another new Movistar title at Mipcom, is a case in point: the TV debut of Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s longtime co-scribe Isabel Peña as a series co-creator.

	“The Castle” shares similarities with “Killing a Bear” and “Celeste.” All three are crime drama-thrillers, the most exportable and ordered of program types, but all three reject tropes of the genre. 

	“Celeste” turns on a dowdy tax fraud inspector. “The Castle” weighs in like “Zodiac” with sex clubs, detailing the long years spent by a young police inspector to bring to justice a prostitution kingpin. “Killing a Bear” is a “fable” that “uses genre as a vehicle to address the violence born of the deeply polarized conflicts over coexistence we see today,” say the Cabezudo brothers, calling the series a procedural.

	Genre provides story tension at a time of general market downturn where series, whatever their hot button issues, must never forget to entertain.

schema.headline: Movistar Plus Drives Into YA Comedy, Smart Social Issue Genre

title: Cambodian Remake of Korean Mother-Daughter Drama ‘Wedding Dress’ Leads Abnormal Studios’ Busan Market Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this yea
body:
A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this year’s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, where the company is selling the film ahead of its local release.

	The new version centers on Dalin, a single mother who designs bridal gowns and whose devotion to her job has opened a gap between her and her 10-year-old daughter Mina. A terminal diagnosis shifts her priorities, and she sets about readying everything she thinks the girl will need for a happy life once she has died.
	

	The Cambodian adaptation is the first feature from Huang Han, whose earlier work has screened at the Berlin, Busan and Pingyao film festivals. It keeps the core of the mother-daughter story while anchoring it in the day-to-day life and emotional textures of the region.


	Also on the slate is “The Hungry One,” Venezuelan horror director Alejandro Hidalgo’s upcoming feature. His credits include “No Voltees” (2024); “The Exorcism of God” (2021), which was distributed in more than 150 countries; and his 2013 breakout “The House at the End of Time,” Venezuela’s top-grossing horror film.

	The story follows Emily, a white American woman whose Chinese husband takes her to visit his relatives’ ancestral home in Malaysia over the 15-day Hungry Ghost Festival, when the boundary with the underworld is lifted and ghosts wander among the living. A mounting series of eerie encounters puts everything she cares about at risk.

	The film is in pre-production, and its producers are working to close the last round of financing.
	

	The company is also handling “Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,” an independent cannibal black comedy-horror from Feisal and Iskander Azizuddin. In it, two friends with nothing to lose become hooked on power after hitting on a winning spicy beef jerky recipe made with human flesh.

	From Malaysia comes sci-fi fantasy “Mimpi Kita: Castle in the Air,” which pits a simulated world against a dystopian real one as it asks what children owe their parents. The project took part in the It Project section of the NAFF Project Market at Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival this year.

	The wider pan-Asian lineup features “Because of You Ka Kui,” a film celebrating Canto rock frontman Wong Ka Kui which, according to the company, has drawn strong fan support in select territories, and “Next Stop, Somewhere,” a drama led by Hong Kong veteran Anthony Wong. From Cambodia comes fish-out-of-water rom-com “Far Away Close to You,” which plays on the might-have-beens of youthful romance.

	Other Southeast Asian titles are “The Ghost of Banana Tree,” adapted from a well-known Cambodian folk horror legend; “Silent Murders,” a crime thriller set in Cambodia’s criminal underworld; “KL Love Story,” an ensemble drama about temptation, loyalty and loneliness in Kuala Lumpur’s after-dark scene; and supernatural horror “Her Deadly Eyes.”

	Indonesian audience favorites round things out, among them the horror franchises “The Doll,” “Mata Batin” and “Rumah Kentang,” and the rom-coms “Sunshine Becomes You” and the “Eiffel… I’m in Love” series.

	Abnormal Studios, a subsidiary of Westec Media Limited, has been acquiring and releasing films since 2020 and has handled more than 400 titles to date. It now puts out around 100 films a year across Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal, with recent hits including “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

schema.headline: Cambodian Remake of Korean Mother-Daughter Drama ‘Wedding Dress’ Leads Abnormal Studios’ Busan Market Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Exorcism of God’ Director Alejandro Hidalgo to Helm Malaysian Hungry Ghost Festival Horror ‘The Hungry One’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia’s Hungry G
body:
Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia’s Hungry Ghost Festival.

	Kuala Lumpur-based Abnormal Studios is handling worldwide sales and is introducing the project at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market. Singapore-based Clover Films has already picked up rights for Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
	

	The story follows Emily, an American woman who travels with Simon, her Chinese Malaysian husband, and their son Louis to spend the summer at his family’s mansion. Their stay coincides with the 15-day festival, when the underworld is believed to open and the dead mingle with the living. Emily becomes the target of escalating encounters with a vengeful presence trying to cross over, and must dig into the house’s hidden past before it takes her family.


	Filmmaker and entrepreneur Justin Leong is driving the project through Los Angeles-based Lightning Pictures.

	“Growing up in Asia, I always felt the Hungry Ghost Festival was incredibly rich visually, from the fire and offerings to the rituals and mythology behind it. When you capture that and shoot it cinematically, it’s movie gold. It gives us a world that audiences may not have seen before, but one that feels immediately atmospheric, mysterious and made for horror,” Leong said.

	Leong, who has deep ties to Malaysian-Chinese culture, drew on his own family’s traditions to shape the story.

	Hidalgo’s first feature, “The House at the End of Time,” remains Venezuela’s biggest horror hit at the box office. It earned strong notices on the festival circuit and has since gathered a cult audience for mixing the supernatural with science fiction. His 2021 follow-up, “The Exorcism of God,” bowed at Fantastic Fest and went on to sell to more than 150 countries, with Saban Films handling its U.S. theatrical release. It ended 2022 as the highest-grossing Latin American film worldwide.
	

	Producer Harrison Allen, who won the live action short Oscar at this year’s Academy Awards for Netflix title “The Singers,” is also on board. His latest feature, “Anima,” screened at SXSW this year. 

	Also attached is Thomas Percy Kim, a Sundance and Toronto fellow whose debut feature “Isle Child,” based on his own short that HBO Max acquired, premiered in Toronto. Screenwriter Justin Parker worked on the development of HBO’s Emmy-nominated limited series “Station Eleven” and was a writer on docuseries “Religion of Sports.”

	“The Hungry One” is in pre-production, with its producers working to lock the last portion of its financing.

	Abnormal Studios, a subsidiary of Westec Media Limited, has been acquiring and releasing films since 2020 and has handled more than 400 titles to date. It now brings around 100 films a year to Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal. Recent releases include “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

title: Michael Douglas Tells Bill Maher About Smuggling Marijuana in Suitcases, Slams ‘Nepo Baby’ Label
description: On Friday night, Michael Douglas stopped by “Real Time with Bill Maher” to promote his mammoth memoir “One Helluva Ride,” chronicling the acclaimed
body:
On Friday night, Michael Douglas stopped by “Real Time with Bill Maher” to promote his mammoth memoir “One Helluva Ride,” chronicling the acclaimed actor and producer’s rise through the Hollywood ranks, from winning the Best Picture Oscar for producing “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” to winning the Best Actor Oscar for “Wall Street” to the present-day.

	The book also covered “sex, drugs and rock and roll,” as he told Maher, including how Douglas helped pay for college by smuggling marijuana across the country in fancy suitcases gifted to him by his actor-father Kirk Douglas.
	

	“You and I share something in common about getting through college together,” offered Douglas, to which Maher replied, “What it is we discovered is that when you buy pot in one place and sell it in a different place, the difference between those two amounts can be very good in living your life.”

	“Especially between East Coast and West Coast,” Douglas added. “When I turned 21, Dad wrote me a check for $10,000 and said, ‘Great son, you’re on your own.’ I said, ‘Well, Dad, this is wonderful, but I’ve got a couple of years of tuition left in school…’”

	So, Douglas took matters into his own hands. “One time I said, ‘Dad, you remember one Christmas you bought me two beautiful Italian soft leather suitcases? Well, I found out that each one of those suitcases could hold 22 kilos of marijuana.’ I would go back east to see my mom with the clothes on my back and two suitcases. This was called BD: Before Dogs.”

	Later on in their talk, the HBO host gave Douglas props for working normal jobs to make money despite having a rich actor as a father, including his time working at a Mobil gas station in Connecticut at the age of 20 and earning the title of “Mobil Man of the Month.” The topic prompted Douglas to address the “nepo baby” discourse, where the children of Hollywood players have been criticized for getting a significant leg up in the industry.
	

	“With this ‘nepo baby’ thing, doesn’t every single business, doesn’t a father or a mother want their son or daughter to go into the business?” he asked, defensively. “They have a sign that says ‘so and so and sons,’ so why pick on show business?”

title: Spain’s TV Powerhouses Forge New Partnerships as Series Biz Evolves
description: Spain’s TV industry is shifting gears as international buyers grow more selective, prompting its leading operators to rethink their series business
body:
Spain’s TV industry is shifting gears as international buyers grow more selective, prompting its leading operators to rethink their series business.

	Pay TV operator Movistar Plus is scaling up in Spanish originals. Atresmedia is strengthening its longstanding relationship with Netflix, while Mediterráneo Mediaset is placing a large emphasis on international sales.
	

	Meanwhile, public broadcasters are pursuing different models of collaboration. RTVE shares financing and rights with overseas partners, while Catalonia’s 3Cat brings partners aboard at the development stage.


	“In a contracted economy and a very saturated market, we have to nurture the international side very carefully,” says Ghislain Barrois, CEO of Mediterráneo Mediaset España Group.


	Barrois sees a shift in the global streamers’ buying priorities. “Now they are focusing much more on local series, and the rest of the market is adapting to that,” he says.

	“Licensing and co-production, too, are again an important tool,” says Guy Bisson, executive director of Ampere Analysis. Both fell out of favor during the peak-TV boom, but successive release windows now offer ways to “extend life and monetization opportunities,” he adds.
	

	Atresmedia is extending the commercial life of its programming through deals with streaming platforms. Its latest Netflix deal brings Antena 3’s daily drama “Dreams of Freedom” to the platform, with Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo‘s “Veneno” also set to join the service. Since  2025, a Disney+ deal brings Spanish subscribers 300-plus hours annually from Atresmedia’s Atresplayer.

	“Rather than a change, what we are doing is consolidating our content distribution strategy,” says José Antonio Antón, general director of Atresmedia.

	The broadcaster has long viewed global streamers “as an ally and not as a threat,” an approach that also informs content development. “We study this strategy carefully to ensure it does not cannibalize our business model but, on the contrary, expands and strengthens it,” Antón says.

	Atresmedia’s recent originals include “Adrift,” from Mediawan’s Boomerang TV and Buendía Estudios Canarias, about fishermen returning after being presumed dead.

	The volume of content Netflix licensed in Spain rose from 2,420 hours in 2024 to 2,829 in 2025, including around 700 hours from RTVE and Atresmedia, up from 543 a year earlier, Ampere Analysis estimates.

	Licensing existing programs is one part of the equation. With production costs rising, broadcasters are also bringing partners together to finance new series and share the investment.

	“The increase in production costs makes it ever more difficult for a single operator to assume the financing of certain projects on its own,” says Rafael Bardem, RTVE’s deputy director of co-productions.

	Alongside sales of finished programs, RTVE uses advance financing agreements that divide territories and exploitation windows among partners. “El Valle del Arcángel,” which involves “Narcos” producer Dynamo and Sony, follows that model. “It is a demanding formula, because it requires developing a product capable of connecting with audiences in different markets,” Bardem says.

	For 3Cat, those partnerships also shape projects from the development stage. “The earlier the principal editorial and financial partners come aboard, the easier it is to accommodate the conditions each considers essential or non-negotiable,” says Pío Vernis, 3Cat’s director of audiovisual business.

	3Cat tailors release arrangements to each production, working with Netflix and Prime Video while seeking a Catalan premiere for projects it leads. “We think and rethink the windowing formula for each production,” Vernis notes.
	

	Charting Ferran Adrià’s culinary revolution at his restaurant El Bulli, drama “Gènesi” has Netflix aboard across multiple territories, with New Regency also handling international distribution outside Spain.

	Over the next three years, Movistar Plus plans to increase its annual output of Spanish originals from eight to 16 series, alongside another 10 titles through co-production and rights acquisition agreements. Recent Movistar Plus co-productions include “Killing a Bear,” with Arte France.

	For Rebeca Aguilar, head of international distribution at Movistar Plus, co-productions offer more than financial backing. “They also provide us with a partner who brings a great deal of value to the series and represents a first step in its international reach,” she says.

	Barrois is more cautious about international co-productions. “From an industrial and economic point of view, if you find someone with whom to share the bill, fantastic. But editorially it is more complicated,” he says. “We design our series with our audience and Spain in mind.”

	Barrois says Spain retains a cost advantage despite rising production expenditures: “I think we are still well below most European countries.”

	Mediaset’s domestic-first approach goes hand-in-hand with international sales and platform partnerships. Its family mystery drama “Pure Bred,” produced with Banijay’s Shine Iberia, has secured distribution across 29 territories, including the U.S., Canada and the U.K. through Walter Presents, plus a Spanish licensing deal with SkyShowtime. Mediterráneo has also sold Bambú-produced period drama “La Favorita” to nearly 100 territories and licensed ITV Studios’ Plano a Plano series “She, Damned Soul” to Movistar Plus.

	On the commissioning front, crime and thrillers lead Spanish-language scripted orders, accounting for 32% of announced VoD commissions in 2025, ahead of comedy at 21% and drama at 20%, according to Ampere Analysis.

	Genre alone does not determine how well a series travels. “The principal factor is good stories which, regardless of whether they are more local or more global, allow viewers in any country” to engage with them and relate to them, says Aguilar.

	Vernis also sees international appeal in the cultural roots of Max Original co-production “Pubertat,” set against Catalonia’s castells, or “human towers” that are built during festivals and celebrations.

	Comedy can be harder to export, Barrois notes, given its reliance on local humor. But format adaptations offer another route: Netflix has commissioned local versions of Contubernio’s Spanish original “Machos Alfa” in markets such as France, Italy and Germany. 3Cat’s “Unfiltered,” a Gen Z-focused short-form series, is also suited to adaptation in other territories.

body:
Kevin Hart To Judge
                          Stop My Sex Tape Partner From Testifying!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 10, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kevin Hart is asking a judge to intervene in his court battle with his ex-assistant, Miesha Shakes ... and he wants to prevent the woman from his infamous sex tape from taking the stand.
      
    
            The comedian filed court docs days after Miesha, who worked for Kevin from 2017 to 2020, named his sex tape partner, Montia Sabbag, as a potential witness who could testify in her case.
      
    
            Miesha said Montia may testify about the scandal and her ensuing legal war with Kevin over the X-rated tape.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Kevin is suing Miesha over an interview she did with blogger Tasha K, where Miesha spoke about his personal life.
      
    
            Kevin claims she violated a non-disclosure agreement she signed when she left his company. For her part, Miesha argues the NDA is not enforceable because she claims Kevin didn't comply with his other obligations under their deal.
      
    
            In his new court docs, obtained by TMZ, Kevin says Miesha did not talk to his legal team about her witness list before submitting it, which he claims is improper.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kevin believes Miesha submitted the witness list naming Montia to embarrass him and create a scandal. He asked the court not to allow Miesha to call irrelevant witnesses like Montia, arguing she has nothing to do with the case at hand. 
      
    
            KH insists only he, Miesha, and Tasha K are relevant to the case, and the others should be barred from testifying unless Miesha can establish their testimony is relevant to the matters in the case.
      
    
            In his lawsuit, Kevin says his reputation was damaged by Miesha's interview with Tasha K. He is seeking unspecified damages.
